## Root cause (systemic, not per-agent)
The worker's `handleDedicatedAgentProxy` → `proxyToOrigin` forwards to `AGENT_ROUTER_ORIGIN_HOST = eliza-staging-1.elizacloud.ai` (the staging CP). The CP runs **nginx** (:80/:443) which routes `<id>.staging.elizacloud.ai` to the agent over the **headscale tailnet** via the agent's `headscale_ip`. But:
- **All 48 running staging agents have `headscale_ip` NULL/empty** (`SELECT (headscale_ip IS NULL OR headscale_ip='') , count(*) FROM agent_sandboxes WHERE status='running'` → `t | 48`).
- **`headscale nodes list` on the CP shows NO online agent-tagged node** — only `cp-staging-router` (tag:eliza-proxy, online) and two `robot-tstest`/`robot-tstest2` (tag:agent) **offline since 2026-06-16**.

So staging agent containers are provisioned + running + serving on their node bridge (`bridge_url` is set, e.g. `http://91.98.38.74:19006`), but they **never join the headscale mesh**, so the CP router has no tailnet address to reach them → 404. The agent's own CORS (`resolveCorsOrigin`, which allows any origin when `ELIZA_CLOUD_PROVISIONED=1`) is never reached because the request dies at the CP hop.

## Why it surfaced only now
Nobody ever got a staging agent reachable end-to-end before tonight (DB split #15160 → image boot #15196 → wildcard/TLS #15205 all had to land first). This is the next distinct gap in the same 'staging never fully mirrored prod' class, adjacent to the known prod-parity headscale gap.

## What to investigate
Why staging agent containers don't join headscale: is the tailscale-up / headscale pre-auth-key step injected at provision time (the staging worker HAS `HEADSCALE_PUBLIC_URL`/`HEADSCALE_API_URL`/`HEADSCALE_USER=tunnel`) actually running in the container, and is the provisioning worker recording `headscale_ip` back to `agent_sandboxes`? Either the join is failing/skipped or the IP is never persisted. Fixing it should light up all 48 agents at once.

_Workstream: **Voice pipeline** · [design doc](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/develop/packages/docs/ongoing-development/research/07-voice-pipeline.md) · [MVP board](https://github.com/orgs/elizaOS/projects/15)_a:T1851,Part of the corpus PII scrub pipeline (multimodal foundation) — and a standalone knowledge-hub improvement.

## Problem

Transcripts already mirror into knowledge and are chunked/embedded like documents, but the mirror is `transcriptPlainText()` (`packages/shared/src/transcripts.ts`), which STRIPS all timing; fragments inherit `transcriptId`/`audioUrl` but have no per-fragment time range. Consequences:

- A search hit cannot seek the stored audio — the player opens at t=0.
- The PII pipeline cannot map a text-PII span found in a fragment back to an audio timestamp span, which `[pii] Audio redaction` requires.
- **Live data-loss bug (prerequisite):** voice-session WAVs are invisible to the media GC. `transcriptKnowledgePayload` sets ONLY `metadata.audioUrl` (`plugins/plugin-local-inference/src/services/voice/transcript-knowledge.ts:66`) while `collectReferencedMedia` scans only `content.attachments[].url`/`thumbnailUrl` + `metadata.mediaUrl` (`packages/agent/src/api/media-runtime.ts:161-193`), so the WAV is swept after the 1h grace on the next daily `MEDIA_GC`. `meeting-transcript-writer.ts:425-432` documents this exact hazard and sets BOTH keys; the voice-session path does not. Timestamps into deleted audio are meaningless.

Producer fidelity today: local fused eliza-1-asr ABI v12 gives per-word ms spans (`asrTranscribeTimed`, `plugins/plugin-local-inference/src/services/voice/ffi-bindings.ts:395/918/2193`); meeting segments carry `words: []` because the seam is the locked string-only `ModelType.TRANSCRIPTION` (`plugins/plugin-meetings/src/pipeline/transcriber.ts` header documents why); the cloud STT route parses only `{text}` and discards all timestamps (`packages/cloud/api/v1/voice/stt/route.ts`).

## Architecture

1. **Pre-chunked ingest seam:** optional `fragments?: Array<{text, metadata: {segmentIds, startMs, endMs, speakerLabels}}>` input on `DocumentService.addDocument` (`packages/core/src/features/documents/service.ts:645`) / `processFragmentsSynchronously` (`packages/core/src/features/documents/document-processor.ts:95`). `fragmentMetadata` already spreads document metadata, so per-fragment `startMs`/`endMs` rides jsonb metadata — zero schema/table change.
2. **Producers chunk on segment boundaries:** `transcriptKnowledgePayload` (`plugin-local-inference/src/services/voice/transcript-knowledge.ts`) and `plugins/plugin-meetings/src/transcripts/meeting-transcript-writer.ts` build ~chunk-size groups from `Transcript.segments` they already hold — never splitting inside a segment.
3. **Project anchors through search:** `/api/documents/search` result mapping (`plugins/plugin-documents/src/routes.ts:785`) adds `transcriptId`, `startMs`, `endMs` next to `documentId`/`position`; same for the `documents` action=search formatter (`packages/core/src/features/documents/actions.ts`) so agent-facing hits carry anchors.
4. **Deep-link playback:** `packages/ui/src/components/pages/documents-detail.tsx` / TranscriptPlayer accept an initial seek (`?t=<ms>` or prop); `flattenTranscriptWords`/`activeWordIndex` already exist — only the entry offset is missing.
5. **GC fix (prerequisite):** set `metadata.mediaUrl = audioUrl` in `transcriptKnowledgePayload` (matching the meeting writer) AND/OR make `collectReferencedMedia` also collect `metadata.audioUrl`.
6. **Producer fidelity (second priority within this issue):**
   - Meetings word timings: expose timed ASR as a real runtime seam — a service or additive typed model registration in plugin-local-inference wrapping `transcribePcmTimed`/`asrTranscribeTimed` — so plugin-meetings' `AsrBackend` can return `words[]` when the fused v12 lib serves. Do NOT widen the locked `ModelType.TRANSCRIPTION` ⇒ string contract; add a parallel typed surface.
   - Cloud STT timestamps: `packages/cloud/api/v1/voice/stt/route.ts` requests `response_format=verbose_json` (+ `timestamp_granularities` where the deployed faster-whisper supports it), parses segments/words, and returns them in the DTO alongside `transcript`.
7. **Edits stay correct for free:** `TranscriptService.update` already deletes + re-adds the mirror; segment-boundary chunking re-derives anchors from patched segments.
8. **Documented caveat, not fixed here:** v12 word timings are duration-proportional char-weighted, not forced alignment — sufficient for seek/highlight anchors; `validateAsrWordTimings` (`packages/shared/src/transcripts.ts`) remains the producer gate.

## Acceptance criteria

- Fragment rows for a mirrored transcript carry `startMs`/`endMs`/`segmentIds`; boundaries never split a segment (unit + integration against real fixture audio — `plugins/plugin-local-inference/native/audio-fixtures/freeman.wav`, harness pattern `asr-timed.real.test.ts`).
- `/api/documents/search` and the `documents` action return `transcriptId` + `startMs` + `endMs`; UI evidence: MP4 walkthrough — search a word, click the hit, the player opens mid-audio at the anchor and the word is audible.
- **GC regression test:** seeded voice-session transcript + WAV → run the referenced-set computation → WAV survives; the test FAILS on current develop behavior.
- Meetings: with the fused v12 lib present, meeting segments carry `words[]` (`*.real.test.ts` lane, skipped-never-faked when the lib/bundle is absent); cloud STT DTO carries segments/words (live contract test precedent: `packages/cloud/api/__tests__/voice-kokoro-whisper-live.test.ts`).
- Transcript edit → re-mirror recomputes anchors (test patches a segment, asserts new fragment ranges).
- Evidence inline in the PR: fragment row dumps, search JSON, deep-link playback video, GC logs (`PR_EVIDENCE.md`).

## Out of scope

The PII scrub itself; audio muting (`[pii] Audio redaction`); any second file store or files/refcount table (#8876); whisper.cpp resurrection (retired — fused eliza-1-asr only); widening `ModelType.TRANSCRIPTION`.

## Pipeline integration

This is the multimodal pipeline's text↔time bridge: the LLM-pass finds PII in fragment text; fragment anchors + word timings convert verdicts to timestamp spans consumed by `[pii] Audio redaction`. Fragments are documents, so the corpus enumeration and `pii:<sha256>:v<ruleset>` idempotency layers apply unchanged.

`app-staging.elizacloud.ai` is stuck on **"initializing agent"** for every new agent. Root cause: **every agent-create call to the staging cloud-api returns HTTP 500 `{"code":"internal_error"}`**. The UI provisions the agent, then polls the per-agent proxy passthrough (`GET /api/conversations`) which never serves (the agent was never created), so `runCloudManagedWarmup()` spins on `initializing-agent` until the warmup deadline.

The 500 is an **unhandled DB/infrastructure error** inside the create handler, forced to the generic `internal_error` envelope by `isInfrastructureError()` in `cloud-worker-errors.ts` (so the real SQLSTATE/SQL message is swallowed to avoid leaking raw SQL).

## Reproduction (staging, authenticated session)
```
POST /api/v1/eliza/agents {"agentName":"x","autoProvision":false}  → 500 internal_error (t≈2–8s)
POST /api/v1/eliza/agents {"agentName":"x","autoProvision":true,"dockerImage":"ghcr.io/elizaos/eliza-agent:latest"} → 500 internal_error (t≈7.6s)
```
Both shared and dedicated create paths 500 → it's the create **write**, not provisioning/worker-health.

## Reads are healthy — this is write/transaction-specific
```
GET /api/v1/eliza/agents    → 200 {"data":[]}   (t spiky 0.27–6.4s, but succeeds)
GET /api/v1/credits/balance → 200 {"balance":…} (t≈1.3s)
GET /api/health             → 200 environment:staging
```
- Bogus `dockerImage` → **403 agent_image_not_allowed** (handler reaches deep into `createAgent`/`assertAgentImageAllowed`; the write AFTER the allowlist gate is what fails).
- `getReadConnection()` and `getWriteConnection()` both resolve the **same** `getPrimaryDatabaseUrl()`/Hyperdrive binding, so this is NOT a code-level read/write DB split. The difference: create runs a **multi-statement interactive `dbWrite.transaction`** with a Postgres advisory lock + `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` + INSERT (`eliza-sandbox.ts` `createAgent`), while a passing read is a single pooled query.

## Ruled out
- **Schema drift** — deploy migrations job: `[db:migrate] pending migrations: 0; migrations complete`; deployed branch has migrations through `0176`.
- **General DB outage** — reads succeed.
- **Deployed branch code** — staging is currently deployed from `fix/cloud-cerebras-reasoning-effort` (PR #16087) via `workflow_dispatch`; that PR touches zero create/sandbox/db-client/managed-env files.

## Most likely cause
Interactive transaction / advisory-lock write over the **staging Hyperdrive binding `ef65eb94c74144a3a3848ad1945571fb`** failing (SQLSTATE swallowed to generic 500), while simple pooled reads pass. Same failure class as the previously-closed #15160 / #15203 staging-provisioning DB incidents.

## Needs (holder-gated — I don't have elizaOS CF account access)
1. `wrangler tail eliza-cloud-api-staging --env staging --format json` while issuing a create, to capture the swallowed Postgres SQLSTATE behind `[CloudApi] Unhandled error`.
2. Verify staging Hyperdrive binding `ef65eb94c74144a3a3848ad1945571fb` points at the intended **staging** Postgres and supports interactive transactions (re-point if stale/misconfigured — the #15160 surface).
3. Consider reverting staging to `develop` (currently on the cerebras feature branch) so QA tests real staging code.

Once the SQLSTATE is known: a code-level Hyperdrive-transaction incompatibility is a bounded fix; a binding/DB-target misconfig is an ops flip.

_Diagnosed by [sol-cloud]. No prod changes, no staging redeploy, no DB writes persisted._

## What we HAVE (verified, more than the incident history suggests)

**Lifecycle state machine** (`packages/cloud/shared/src/db/schemas/agent-sandboxes.ts`): `pending → provisioning → running`, plus `stopped` (suspend: container removed, slot freed, DB kept), `sleeping` (cold storage: durable backup then teardown, zero compute), `disconnected`, `error`, `deletion_pending/failed`. Driven by a jobs queue with 3 retries + stale-job recovery, executed by the `provisioning-worker` daemon (`packages/scripts/cloud/admin/daemons/provisioning-worker.ts`), which is the live orchestrator (the `container-control-plane` sidecar is effectively deprecated).

**Crash recovery, today**: containers run with `--restart unless-stopped` + Docker HEALTHCHECK (`docker-sandbox-provider.ts:1254-1263`); heartbeat loop probes `/api/health` over headscale with hysteresis → `disconnected` (`eliza-sandbox.ts:4218-4287`) → `dedicated-always` agents get re-probed and idempotently re-provisioned (`provisioning-jobs.ts:2939-2972`); stuck-`provisioning` rows are reconciled (`:3004`); nodes get SSH health checks with auto-disable after N consecutive failures + autoscaler replacement (`docker-node-manager.ts:317-428`); the daemon has a watchdog self-restart under systemd + an external Redis-heartbeat monitor that alerts when the daemon itself dies.

**Backups, today**: `agent_sandbox_backups` with full/incremental, manifest covering DB (pglite-files or postgres-rows) + media + vault + character + state-dir, KMS-AES-256-GCM encryption, 6-hourly auto-backup cron + retention pruning, `pre-shutdown`/`pre-upgrade` snapshots, restore-on-wake, and a daemon boot-refusal on ephemeral `memory` KMS (the countermeasure to the incident below).

**Deactivation, today**: suspend/resume and sleep/wake job types + API routes exist (`v1/eliza/agents/[agentId]/{suspend,resume,sleep,wake}`); billing-driven auto-suspend on credit exhaustion with 48h warning exists. What does NOT exist is any user-facing product surface for it.

**CI, today**: mock-lane coverage is broad (~130 cloud-api PGlite unit tests, 16 server-backed e2e groups, full-journey Playwright suite over a mock stack incl. provision/deprovision/sleep-wake/suspend-resume/scheduled-backup); real-infra coverage is `hetzner-e2e.yml` nightly (provision → deploy trivial agent via staging API → `status.get` ping → teardown) + a 30-min leak reaper + `hetzner-sleep-wake-smoke.yml` (provision A → backup → **destroy A** → provision B → restore → verify) which is **dispatch-only**.

Trajectory recording can attribute an outcome to the FINAL prompt but cannot decompose that prompt into provider contributions — the single fact blocking any learned optimization of context composition (provider selection/order/rendering/budgets) and any per-provider cost/win accounting. Provider accesses are logged length-only; the joined providers block sits undifferentiated inside the recorded prompt string; provider order is computed in-memory and never persisted.

## Current state (refs, worktree-verified)

- `logProviderAccess` records `data: { textLength }` only (`packages/core/src/runtime.ts:4273`); `TrajectoryProviderAccessRecord` (`packages/core/src/services/trajectory-types.ts:130`) has no text, hash, or token count.
- `state.data.providerOrder` exists in-memory (`runtime.ts:4377`, consumed at `:7883-7890`) but is never stamped onto the recorded LLM call.
- No span offsets map prompt regions back to providers; no tokenizer pass over provider text; no (provider -> cost, marginal delta-judgeScore) ledger anywhere (`context-audit.ts` audits only context-category mapping; `recordInferenceSpan` captures latency only).
- The access LIST is already complete: while a trajectory step records, provider-cache reuse is disabled so every requested provider re-executes (`runtime.ts:4149-4164`) — capture fidelity is not the problem, record shape is.
- Everything else per call is already captured (full prompt, messages, tools, usage, costUsd — `runtime/trajectory-recorder.ts`; DB twin `trajectory-types.ts:85`), and judge rewards ride into datasets (`metadata.judge_score`, #8795).

## Proposed

1. Extend the provider-access record with `{ sha256, tokenCount, position, spanStart, spanEnd }` (text itself optional/hash-first to keep privacy-filter semantics; spans reference the recorded prompt string of the consuming call).
2. Stamp `providerOrder` (and the applied selection set) onto each `RecordedModelCall`/`TrajectoryLlmCallRecord` produced from that composeState.
3. Tokenizer pass at record time (same tokenizer family the batcher uses) for per-provider `tokenCount`; roll into a per-provider cost ledger derivable from existing `costUsd`.
4. Composition-aware replay groundwork: with spans + order persisted, a replay harness can re-render candidate (selection, order, template, budget) configs against recorded provider state — the inner loop for the GEPA-over-dynamic-context issue; `packages/scripts/trajectory.ts` gains a `providers` view (per-provider tokens/cost per call).
5. Keep the recording gate semantics unchanged (`runtime/trajectory-gate.ts`); size impact bounded by hash-first storage.

## Acceptance criteria + evidence bar

- A live recorded trajectory (scenario-runner, real model, read by hand) shows per-provider `{sha256, tokenCount, position, spanStart, spanEnd}` on each LLM call, and slicing the recorded prompt by the spans reproduces each provider's text exactly (round-trip test).
- `trajectory.ts` prints a per-provider token/cost table for a real trajectory; provider set + order reconstructable from the record alone (fixture test over a multi-provider compose).
- No behavior change when trajectory logging is off; privacy filter still strips provider text where required (hash retained).

## Out of scope

The optimizer/genome work and the ablation runner (parent GEPA issue); report rendering (reports issue); DB schema migrations beyond the trajectory record shape.

11:T17d0,## Summary

The Cloud chat gateway still adds seconds before a Cerebras request despite the provider itself being fast. A paired staging benchmark now isolates the dominant regression: chat crosses **three Railway-TCP Redis rate-limit gates** before provider forwarding. After 30 seconds idle, the two Hono middleware gates alone add **2.45–3.11s** outside the route timer, and the handler's org gate contributes to another **0.51–0.97s** phase. Direct Cerebras remains **0.09–0.37s**.

This is not reasoning-effort overhead and it is not slow Cerebras generation. The actual gateway-to-Cerebras response-header phase was **0.09–0.33s** in every post-idle case.

## Live evidence

Accepted paired run (staging gateway and direct provider, same prompts/models, paced below limits):

- Run: https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/29167994915
- Job: https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/29167994915/job/86584408510
- Artifact: https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/29167994915/artifacts/8252811951
- 320/320 HTTP 200; 0 transport failures; 0 SSE terminal failures
- 160 gateway + 160 direct samples; 30 warm pairs per case plus cold/post-idle
- Both paths entered Cloudflare at IAD; every gateway inference used the direct pass-through path

Post-idle gateway decomposition (`response headers - route total` exposes middleware before the route timer):

| Model/case | Outside route | Auth | Mid reads | Reserve | Provider-to-headers | Gateway headers |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Gemma / none | 2,993ms | 151ms | 664ms | 812ms | 333ms | 4,953ms |
| GLM / omit | 2,540ms | 158ms | 659ms | 844ms | 89ms | 4,290ms |
| GLM / none 4096 | 3,100ms | 44ms | 965ms | 755ms | 161ms | 5,025ms |
| Gemma / omit | 2,450ms | 1,827ms | 514ms | 614ms | 89ms | 5,494ms |
| GLM / none 512 | 3,107ms | 34ms | 862ms | 789ms | 156ms | 4,948ms |

The matched direct samples returned headers/TTFT in 86–365ms.

Warm gateway p50 was still 485ms vs direct headers around 81–88ms, with gateway outliers up to 5.84s. The hidden outside-route interval reached 4.66s.

### Independent live-tail confirmation on current staging

On commit `b2e36d3`, privacy-safe unauthenticated chat probes reproduced both modes without ever calling a model provider:

- successful Railway Redis check: 556–589ms wall
- SocketRedis timeout: 2.378s, 3.250s, and 3.459s wall
- exact log: `SocketRedis operation timed out after 1000ms`
- degraded response policy: `redis-unavailable` (the limiter fell open)

Across 679 successful Worker requests in the prior 30 minutes, p95 wall time was 3.40s and p99 was 8.49s. `/api/health`, which bypasses the lazy full-app import, stayed at 0–1ms; cold chat also pays initialization for the monolithic 580-route app.

## Code-level cause

Every chat call currently stacks:

1. `bootstrap-app.ts`: global Hono IP limiter (600/min), before the chat route timer.
2. `v1/chat/completions/route.ts`: Hono API-key limiter (200/min), also before the timer.
3. `handleChatCompletionsPOST`: per-org tier limiter (60/120/300 per minute).

All three use `REDIS_URL` in staging/production. `redis-factory.ts` resolves that to `SocketRedis` over `cloudflare:sockets`, opening request-scoped TCP/TLS connections to Railway. The committed Wrangler comments simultaneously state that raw external Redis from Workers is unreliable and can hang under load. `SocketRedis` has a 1,000ms operation timeout, so the measured two outer stalls plus one inner stall match the three connection/operation failure windows. Its error cleanup awaits an unbounded `close()` sequence, so the documented 1s ceiling is not actually a wall-clock ceiling; that is consistent with 3–4.66s outside-route outliers.

The existing `X-Eliza-Preforward-Ms` header starts inside `handleChatCompletionsPOST`, so it cannot see the largest two gates and currently labels provider-header wait as `total`. This is tracked more broadly in #16079.

## Required fix

- Replace the protective global and chat route Redis gates with Cloudflare's native Rate Limiting binding. It is machine-local/non-network-blocking and designed for protective limits.
- Keep the organization-tier limit on a globally strong backend. Cloudflare's native binding is location-local and eventually consistent, so silently substituting it would weaken the purchased org quota. Batch its lease reconciliation and use one request-scoped connection or a strong Cloudflare primitive such as a Durable Object.
- Preserve explicit 429 behavior and observable policy headers/logs. Missing/misconfigured production bindings must fail visibly, not silently disable protection.
- Bound SocketRedis teardown so an operation timeout remains a real wall-clock ceiling for non-chat consumers.
- Extend correlated telemetry across global limiter, route limiter, auth, org tier lookup/limit, pool selection, balance gate/reservation, provider fetch-to-headers, first byte/token, stream completion, and deferred settlement.
- Keep production untouched until staging proves the change.

## Acceptance criteria

- Unit/integration tests cover allow, deny, binding failure/missing binding, batched lease reconciliation, and no duplicate counter increments.
- Wrangler dry-run and generated binding types pass for staging and production config.
- A real staging paired run repeats the same five Cerebras cases with at least 30 warm pairs/case plus 30-second post-idle probes, paced below limits.
- Post-idle paired excess outside the route timer (`gateway headers - route total - matched direct headers`) has p90 below 100ms, and no Redis TCP timeout appears in the two protective chat ingress limiters.
- Gateway provider-to-headers remains within 2x direct after subtracting deliberate auth/billing work; all remaining deltas are named by truthful telemetry.
- Billing reservations/deferred settlement, auth failures, 402s, and 429s retain their existing correctness semantics.

Related: #9899 (original pre-forward work, now shown incomplete for middleware), #15513 (Smart Placement), #16079 (truthful E2E telemetry), #16137 (paired live harness).
12:T8c1,## Problem

`computeEffectiveMaxTokens` currently applies:

`Math.max(request.max_tokens, 4096)`

to every model classified as using reasoning tokens. Both pass-through and SDK paths send that raised value upstream.

A client requesting `max_tokens:512` therefore authorizes an upstream ceiling of 4096 without any response field or header indicating that the request was changed.

The controlled Gemma/GLM latency run discovered this because direct requests used 512 while the gateway silently sent 4096, invalidating the original comparison.

## Why this is delicate

The floor was intentionally introduced by #8189/#8486 to prevent reasoning models from consuming a low budget entirely in hidden reasoning and returning an empty but billed answer. It must not simply be deleted.

Nevertheless, silently increasing an explicit caller ceiling is an API-contract and money-integrity problem: it can permit more generation, reservation, and spend than the caller requested.

## Required decision

Choose and document one safe contract:

1. Preserve an explicit caller cap; only apply a default floor when the field is absent.
2. Reject a reasoning-enabled request whose cap is too small with a clear 4xx.
3. Permit a low cap when reasoning is explicitly disabled.
4. Introduce explicit answer-vs-reasoning budget semantics.

Whichever contract is selected, expose requested and effective values in bounded telemetry and ensure billing admission uses the same effective value sent upstream.

## Acceptance

- An explicit output ceiling is never silently increased.
- Low-budget reasoning requests cannot regress to misleading `finish_reason:"stop"` with empty billed content.
- GLM-4.7 with `reasoning_effort:"none"` can use a genuinely small budget.
- Streaming and non-streaming routes behave consistently.
- Reservations and final billing are tested against the exact provider-facing budget.
- The benchmark harness records both requested and effective budgets.
- Compatibility behavior is documented.

## References

- Original broad floor: #8189
- Launch-model detection extension: #8486
- Equivalent `/v1/messages` history: #12864 / #12865
- Cerebras Chat Completions:
  https://inference-docs.cerebras.ai/api-reference/chat-completions
13:Te0e,## Problem

We cannot currently explain a slow chat turn from one correlated production trace.

The live `X-Eliza-Preforward-Ms` header is also semantically incorrect. The structured log freezes `totalMs` before provider dispatch, but the response header recomputes it after awaiting the streaming handler, which already waited for the provider response. It therefore includes provider-to-headers time while claiming to represent only pre-forward work. Outer Hono/global rate-limit work is not included at all.

This produced incorrect conclusions such as attributing a 6.8s Gemma first-token result entirely to gateway pre-forward work.

## Required trace

Mint one bounded, validated trace ID and propagate it through:

browser → dedicated proxy → agent route → plugin runtime → Cloud API Worker → Cerebras request → first reasoning/content frame → stream completion

Record monotonic boundaries for:

- browser dispatch, response headers, first SSE event, first reasoning delta, first visible content, `[DONE]`
- global limiter and route/API-key limiter
- auth KV/cache and authoritative auth
- organization lookup and organization limiter
- app authorization, credential pool, catalog/pricing, moderation, balance/admission
- provider fetch start, response headers, first upstream frame, first reasoning delta, first content delta, stream completion
- background billing settlement separately from user-visible response time
- Cloudflare colo and `cf-placement`

Do not log prompts, API keys, authorization headers, or unbounded attacker-controlled identifiers.

## Persistence

- Enable sampled Workers traces with custom spans.
- Write aggregate latency events to Workers Analytics Engine.
- Preserve app trace IDs because Cloudflare native trace context is not propagated to external providers.
- Store provider completion/request IDs where Cerebras exposes them.
- Poll Cerebras organization metrics for queue time, TTFT, TPOT, cache rate, and end-to-end latency.

## Benchmark harness

The harness must:

- randomize model and direct/gateway ordering
- use the same prompt, effective token budget, reasoning controls, credential/service tier, and client region
- distinguish cold, warm, and post-idle requests
- collect at least 30 samples per model/path
- report p50/p90/p95 for headers, first event, first visible token, and completion
- retain redacted JSON evidence tied to deployed Worker version

14:T449,Found during adversarial review of #16002 (finding F3, pre-existing gap — not introduced by that PR).

`packages/core/src/features/documents/service.ts` writes the parent DOCUMENT row (`createMemory(memoryWithScope, DOCUMENTS_TABLE)`) **before** `processFragmentsSynchronously`, and the `addDocument` catch only logs and rethrows — there is no `deleteMemory` compensation. So while **validation-time** failures now persist nothing (fixed by #16002's pre-write `validatePreChunkedFragments` hoist), an **embed-time** failure (model down, embedding dimension mismatch) still leaves an orphaned zero-fragment document row in the index: visible in document lists, unmatchable in fragment search.

The failure is at least observable now (typed throw + `runtime.reportError` at the mirrors), but the orphan row remains.

**Fix options:** compensating `deleteMemory` of the parent row in the failure path of `addDocument` (preferred — restores all-or-nothing at the document level), or a reconciliation sweep that removes zero-fragment DOCUMENT rows older than a grace window.

## 1. Discord login failure at boot is terminal — no retry

A transient network blip at exactly the wrong moment produced:

```
Registered Discord message connector for account default
Warn  Failed to login to Discord account default: The socket connection was closed unexpectedly.
Debug [PLUGIN:DISCORD] Discord client ready promise rejected (already logged above) (accountId=default, …)
```

…and the bot then ran for **19 minutes fully deaf** — process `active`, task scheduler humming, zero inbound processing — until a manual restart. discord.js reconnects fine once a gateway session exists; the gap is the **initial** `login()` rejection, which is never retried. A connector whose transport failed to establish should retry with backoff (and keep retrying), not settle into a permanently-connected-looking corpse. The memory-watchdog precedent (#10197) applies: surface + self-heal via the existing restart/retry seams.

## 2. Inbound message ~2.5 min after boot silently dropped — zero trace

After the recovery restart (`Discord client ready for account default` at 23:51:09):

- **23:53:46** — a mention arrives (`use a coding agent to write countdown.py …`). **No trace whatsoever**: no `Processing message`, no triage decision, no staleness tag, nothing. The message is visible in channel history; the bot never saw it or dropped it pre-log.
- **00:00:22** — an identical-format mention (`what is 3 plus 4`) processes instantly and answers.
- Re-sending the identical countdown prompt later: routed `coding → elizaos`, completed clean in 37s.

So there is a window after `ready` (room/world sync? backfill?) where a live inbound message can be dropped **with no log line at any level**. Whatever the gating condition is, a dropped inbound must at least log at Warn with the reason — silent drops are indistinguishable from user error.

16:T1809,Part of the corpus PII scrub pipeline — extends it to audio. Depends on `[pii] Transcript fragments with time anchors` (anchors + the audioUrl GC fix).

## Problem

Text scrubbing leaves PII audible in stored recordings (voice sessions, meetings). Needed: word-timestamp-aligned muting/bleeping that preserves duration (so every transcript anchor stays valid), a redacted variant stored as a second content-addressed object — original for OWNER/ADMIN, redacted for everyone else, composing with the permissioning epic — and a re-transcribe-verify loop proving the PII is actually inaudible.

## Architecture

- **Span production:** timed ASR per-word `{text, startMs, endMs}` via `eliza_inference_asr_transcribe_timed` (ABI v12 — `plugins/plugin-local-inference/src/services/voice/ffi-bindings.ts:395/918/1515/2193`, `timedAsrSupported()` gate; real-audio contract test `asr-timed.real.test.ts`). Text-PII verdicts from the LLM-pass over anchored transcript fragments merge onto word spans → `[{startMs, endMs}]` with padding. Pseudonym labels for spans come from the corpus map (`[pii] Context-retrieval pass`) so audio and text redaction agree on identity.
- **Mute op (empirically verified on ffmpeg 8.1.1):** `ffmpeg -i in -af "volume=0:enable='between(t,S1,E1)+between(t,S2,E2)+...'" -c:a <codec> out` — spans compose by summing `between()` terms. Bleep variant: `-f lavfi -i "sine=f=1000"` + `filter_complex` `amix duration=first`. Measured: WAV → exact duration, −91 dB true silence in span; OGG/opus → exact; M4A/AAC → +1 trailing encoder frame — assert duration with ±(1024/sampleRate)s tolerance or normalize through WAV. Sample count within the stream never changes, so span coordinates remain valid in the redacted variant.
- **Runtime capability:** ffmpeg is desktop/server-only (`packages/agent/src/runtime/core-plugins.ts:168`, `packages/core/src/runtime-env.ts:410` — iOS/Android/workers have none); probe like `whichBin('ffmpeg')` in `plugins/plugin-local-inference/src/services/voice/mic-source.ts`. The voice pipeline's native format is 16 kHz mono PCM16 WAV (`ASR_SAMPLE_RATE`), so pure-TS PCM sample zeroing covers WAV with no ffmpeg at all; ffmpeg is the lane for lossy formats. Hosted option: a `media-redact` Railway sibling of `packages/cloud/services/voice-whisper-stt` (same Dockerfile/railway.toml/live-test pattern) — workerd cannot run ffmpeg, cloud-api may only orchestrate.
- **Storage (#8876-clean):** redacted bytes → `persistMediaBytes` (`packages/agent/src/api/media-store.ts:291`) → new sha256 object at `${STATE_DIR}/media/<sha256'>.<ext>`, served at `/api/media/<sha256'>.<ext>`. No new store, no files table, no fileId. Additive optional `Media` field only (sanctioned by the additive-widening block at `packages/core/src/types/primitives.ts:243-249`), e.g. `redactedOf?: string` (source sha) or `variant?: "redacted"`.
- **Permissioning (composes with the epic):** media bytes are served pre-auth — the sha256 is the capability — so enforcement lives at REFERENCE DISTRIBUTION, not the serve path: the transcript/document DTO carries the ORIGINAL sha URL only for `Role.OWNER`/`ADMIN` (`packages/core/src/types/environment.ts:43-51`; `packages/agent/src/api/boundary-role-resolver.ts`), the redacted sha for everyone else; the original hash must never enter non-privileged message records/context. GC: `gcUnreferencedMedia` (`media-store.ts:503`) keeps each variant alive only while referenced.
- **Re-transcribe-verify loop:** redacted bytes → `runtime.useModel(ModelType.TRANSCRIPTION, {audio, transcriptionPurpose: "interim"})` (`TranscriptionParams`, `packages/core/src/types/model.ts:940-952`; local handler = fused eliza-1-asr; `AsrUnavailableError` ⇒ the verify step FAILS, never a vacuous pass) → assert (a) every PII token ABSENT — exact + normalized fuzzy match, NOT transcript equality (Whisper-family models hallucinate filler over silence), and (b) sentinel non-PII words still PRESENT (over-mute guard). Cloud variant: POST the redacted file to voice-whisper-stt `/v1/audio/transcriptions`.
- Text-side precedent: trajectory redaction (`packages/agent/src/runtime/trajectory-internals.ts:1304` `redactTrajectoryParams`).

## Acceptance criteria

- E2E on real audio: fixture WAV (freeman.wav or a purpose-recorded fixture with planted PII) → spans → mute AND bleep variants across wav/ogg/m4a; per-codec duration assertions; `volumedetect` proves ≤ −85 dB in muted windows.
- **Redacted-audio artifact opened and LISTENED to by a human** — attach the redacted audio inline in the PR (MP4) with a note of what was heard. Hard evidence gate.
- Re-transcribe-verify test in the `*.real.test.ts` lane (skipped-never-faked when `ELIZA_INFERENCE_LIBRARY`/`ELIZA_ASR_BUNDLE` absent): PII absent, sentinels present; a deliberately broken run (one span omitted) FAILS the verify.
- Role test: OWNER DTO carries the original URL; USER/GUEST DTO carries only the redacted URL; a scan proves the original sha never appears in non-privileged room records.
- GC test: both variants referenced → both survive; original dereferenced (retention state flipped) → original collected, redacted survives.
- Idempotency: same input sha + same spans + same ruleset version ⇒ identical output sha; the pipeline done-marker makes re-runs no-ops.
- Constrained-runtime behavior: without ffmpeg, WAV redaction still works (pure-TS zeroing) and lossy-format redaction fails observably (typed error via `runtime.reportError`), never silently skipped.

## Out of scope

Video/image redaction; live/streaming redaction; any files/refcount table (#8876); serve-path auth changes (the capability model stands); forced-alignment ASR upgrades (char-weighted timing is the documented baseline).

## Pipeline integration

Extends the corpus pipeline to multimodal: LLM-pass verdicts (with corpus-consistent pseudonym labels from the context pass) become timestamp spans via the transcript-anchor issue; execution rides `[pii] Async scrub job rails` and the shared `pii:<sha256>:v<ruleset>` idempotency layer; the variant swap is the audio analog of the text write-back stage.

1. `_router.generated.ts` statically imports and mounts the entire 646-route API.

3. Chat-reachable service imports use the repository barrel, pulling unrelated repositories and SDKs.

5. Public chat passes global auth's allowlist immediately, but static imports still pull the full Steward/session/admin graph.

1. Add a feature-flagged inference entry in the thin Worker entrypoint and dispatch only the exact canonical/compatibility inference paths before `getApp()`.
2. Preserve the existing request shell: Cloud/DB/R2 contexts, request ID, CORS, security/no-store headers, structured observation, error mapping, auth, rate limiting, billing, streaming, aborts, and deferred settlement.
3. Move protected-only auth/audit imports behind their branch, use direct repository imports, make `CacheClient.instanceId` request-lazy, and remove/stub Worker-inapplicable dependencies from this entry.
4. If parsing remains material, deploy an internal `eliza-cloud-inference-{staging,prod}` Worker behind a Service Binding. Deploy target first, caller/binding second, and retain a one-flag fallback through soak.

Do not merge a naive static chat-route entry: the current global-scope `randomUUID()` fails Worker startup and must be made request-lazy first.

18:Tc11,Sibling to #16021 (which fixed the *create*-path orphan). The **edit** path (`DocumentService.updateDocument`) has a strictly worse, non-atomic failure mode: an embed-time failure during re-fragmentation **destroys the document's existing, working fragments** and leaves the parent row showing the new content with **zero fragments** — data loss on edit, not just an orphan on create.

## Root cause

`packages/core/src/features/documents/service.ts` `updateDocument` performs a destructive re-fragmentation in this order:

1. `runtime.updateMemory(...)` — overwrites the parent `DOCUMENT` row with the **new** content/metadata.
2. Deletes **every existing fragment** for the document (`deleteMemory` in a loop over `relatedFragments`).
3. `splitAndCreateFragments(...)` then `processDocumentFragmentsBatched(fragments, { continueOnError: false })` — re-embeds and persists the new fragments.

Step 3 embeds via `addEmbeddingToMemory → useModel(TEXT_EMBEDDING)`. When the embedding backend is unavailable or returns a dimension/shape mismatch — the exact failure class #16021 addressed for the create path — `processDocumentFragmentsBatched` with `continueOnError: false` **throws**. But by then:

- the old (working) fragments are already **deleted**, and
- the parent row already holds the **new** text.

Result: the document is now **searchable-empty** (parent visible in lists, unmatchable in fragment/vector/BM25 search) **and the previously-working fragments are permanently gone**. The caller (`documents` action `handleEdit`, and `plugin-documents` PATCH route) gets a thrown error, but the store is already corrupted — there is no compensation and no snapshot to restore.

## Why #16021's fix does not cover this

#16021 / PR #16103 add all-or-nothing compensation to the **create** path (`addDocument`/`processDocument`): on embed failure the freshly-written parent row is rolled back. `updateDocument` is a separate method with a *mutating* sequence (overwrite parent + delete old fragments **before** the new embeds), so it needs a different, snapshot-based repair, not a parent-row delete.

## Acceptance

- An embed-time (or fragment-persist) failure during `updateDocument` must **not** leave the document with fewer fragments than it had before, and must **not** silently swap in the new content while dropping all fragments.
- Preferred: stage the new fragments first (embed + validate before any destructive delete/overwrite), and only swap parent content + delete-old + insert-new once the new fragments are known-good; on failure, the pre-edit state is preserved and a typed `ElizaError` propagates. (A snapshot/restore of the old fragments + parent content is an acceptable alternative.)
- Surface the failure via `runtime.reportError("DocumentService.updateDocument", …)` consistent with #16021.
- Add fails-before/passes-after coverage: embed-down during re-fragmentation, fragment-persist throw, and a healthy edit (must still re-fragment). Prove old fragments survive on failure.

Found during post-#16021 review of the documents mutation surface.
19:T9dc,## Fleet coordination — issues + board discipline (Jul 5)

115 open issues. Multiple agents + humans working the same repo around the clock, different waking hours. This issue is the shared protocol so we don't collide or duplicate. Applies to everyone: humans, Sol's fleet, nubs' agents, shaw's lanes.

### The protocol
1. **Claim before you code.** Assign yourself OR add a `claimed:<name>` label. Anything unclaimed is fair game; anything claimed is off-limits without a comment first.
2. **Check open PRs before starting an issue.** A large share of wasted work is "already fixed in an open PR." `gh pr list --state open` takes 5 seconds.
3. **Link PRs to issues** (`Fixes #N` in the body) so merges auto-close and the board stays true.
4. **Close what you merge.** If your PR supersedes someone's issue, close it with a receipt (what landed, which commit).
5. **`needs-human` (60 issues) = human-only lane**: on-device QA, launch decisions, account/keys. Agents don't touch these; humans should burn this list down.
6. **The other ~45 are codeable-now**: oldest real bugs first. If you take one, claim it (rule 1).
7. **Draft PRs are taken over, not rewritten.** Finish the author's design, push to their branch, mark ready. If you disagree with the design, comment, don't fork it.
8. **Board hygiene is everyone's job**: move your own cards. Automated sync runs hourly and closes superseded issues with receipts, but don't rely on it.

1a:T86ae,Work item **B7** of epic #15603 ("Off-box protection for local-PGlite/host-volume state"). Design only — read-only research against `develop` @ 2026-07-09; all file:line refs verified. **v2** — revised per the [adversarial critique](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/issues/15783#issuecomment-4929917326); changelog at the bottom.

**Problem.** A dedicated agent's entire persistent state lives on a single Hetzner node's local disk. The only off-box copy is a live `/api/snapshot` HTTP pull from the *running* agent, taken 6-hourly (auto cron) plus at sleep/upgrade — **and only agents whose image actually serves that route get even that** (see loss windows below). If the node's disk dies between snapshots, everything since the last backup is gone; if it dies before the first snapshot ever succeeds, everything is gone. There is no node-level volume snapshot or replication for agent containers.

---

## 1. Current-state map

### Where state lives, per execution tier

Execution tiers: `shared | dedicated-lazy | dedicated-always | custom` (`packages/cloud/shared/src/db/schemas/agent-sandboxes.ts:88`).

| Tier / mode | DB state | Files (media, vault, config, workspace) | On-box exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **shared** (default for new agents) | shared cloud Postgres (Railway) | n/a (container-free) | none — off-box by construction |
| **dedicated, `ELIZA_AGENT_LOCAL_STATE=1`** (default for provisioned containers since #8696) | **PGlite at `/root/.eliza/.pgdata`** → host `/data/agents/<agentId>/eliza/.pgdata` | media store `/root/.eliza/media`, vault files, `eliza.json`, state-dir misc, `/app/data` workspace — all on the same host dir | **everything** on one node's local disk |
| **dedicated, `ELIZA_AGENT_LOCAL_STATE=0`** (legacy/opt-out) | shared Postgres via injected `DATABASE_URL` (`database_uri` mode) | same host volume as above | files only; DB off-box |

Key refs:
- Bind mounts: `-v /data/agents/<id>:/app/data` and `-v /data/agents/<id>/eliza:/root/.eliza` — `packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/docker-sandbox-provider.ts:1313-1314`; host path from `getVolumePath()` — `docker-sandbox-utils.ts:429-434`.
- Local-state default + `PGLITE_DATA_DIR=/root/.eliza/.pgdata`: `managed-eliza-config.ts:279-287`. Rationale for the default (shared-Postgres "too many clients" #8696 + ~166 ms/query Railway latency dominating dedicated-chat turns) is documented at `managed-eliza-config.ts:222-236`.
- `database_uri` mode selector: `computeManagedAgentDbEnv()` — `eliza-sandbox.ts:452-478`; `database_uri` is the shared Railway `DATABASE_URL` (`provisionAgentDatabase()` — `eliza-sandbox.ts:6183-6204`; column at `schemas/agent-sandboxes.ts:115`).

### The backup pipeline, today

- Agent-side `POST /api/snapshot` (`packages/agent/src/api/server.ts:2013`) → `createAgentSnapshot()` (`packages/agent/src/services/agent-backup.ts:722-790`): a manifest with per-component sha256 covering the DB (**PGlite `dumpDataDir("gzip")` under `runExclusive`** — `agent-backup.ts:626-657` — a *consistent* logical dump, or `postgres-rows` when on shared DB), the content-addressed media store, vault files, character+config, and remaining state-dir files, all base64 in one JSON body.
- Control-plane pull: `fetchSnapshotState()` (`eliza-sandbox.ts:5958-6004`), 120 s timeout (`:353`), **no size cap** — the pull is always the *full* state even though storage may be incremental.
- Storage: `agent_sandbox_backups.state_data` jsonb in the cloud Postgres, KMS-AES-256-GCM field-encrypted under the org DEK (`db/crypto/agent-backups.ts`), full-or-incremental planning (`eliza-sandbox.ts:4161-4215`), retention `MAX_BACKUPS = 10` (`eliza-sandbox.ts:327`) via chain-safe `pruneBackups` (`db/repositories/agent-sandboxes.ts:1346-1370`).
- Cadence: cron `0 */6 * * *` (`packages/cloud/api/wrangler.toml:60`) → `v1/cron/agent-backups/route.ts` (tunable `?intervalMs=&max=`) → `enqueueScheduledBackups()` default `minIntervalMs = 6h`, `maxAgents = 200` per tick (`provisioning-jobs.ts:1476-1530`). Plus `pre-shutdown` at sleep (`executeSleep` — `eliza-sandbox.ts:4955-5060`; sleep **fails closed** if no durable backup can be captured or found) and `pre-upgrade` snapshots.
- **The route is not universally deployed.** The codebase asserts present-tense that "the deployed elizaOS (V2) agent image … does not expose the bridge `/api/snapshot` route — only the cloud-agent template image (and the in-memory test double) do" (`eliza-sandbox.ts:317-324`). Snapshot attempts against such agents return the `SNAPSHOT_ENDPOINT_UNSUPPORTED` sentinel and are treated as a benign skip (`eliza-sandbox.ts:325`, `:4125-4133`).
- The agent can also write **local** KMS-encrypted backup envelopes (`*.agent-backup.json` under the state dir, `createLocalAgentBackup` — `agent-backup.ts:865`) — but those land on the *same* host volume, so they add nothing against node loss today. They are also written with a plain `fs.writeFile` (`agent-backup.ts:875`) — **not** tmp+rename — which matters the moment anything starts sweeping that spool off-box (§3 Phase 3).

### Exact loss windows per failure mode (local-state dedicated agent)

| Failure | What survives | Durability loss | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Container crash** | host volume intact; `--restart unless-stopped` (`docker-sandbox-provider.ts:1295`) + Docker healthcheck (`:1300-1304`) restart it | ≈ 0 (in-flight writes only; PGlite recovers like power loss) | availability risk is the PGlite stale-lock crash-loop (#11222 → #15228), not durability |
| **Node crash / reboot (disk survives)** | volume intact; containers restart on boot | 0 **if the container resumes on the same node**. If the control plane instead re-provisions to another node, restore comes from the last backup → **silent rewind of up to 6 h+** even though the disk was fine | heartbeat → `disconnected` → `dedicated-always` re-provision path (`provisioning-jobs.ts:2939-2972`) makes this rewind reachable in practice |
| **Node disk loss / node death** | only `agent_sandbox_backups` rows in cloud Postgres | **route-bearing agents: everything since the last successful snapshot — up to 6 h + sweep/queue latency in the best case. Route-less agents: unbounded — total loss of all state since provisioning** | this is the B7 gap |

Worst cases that make the window unbounded or the cadence a fiction:

1. **Never-backed-up agents (route-less images).** The sweep only enqueues rows with `bridge_url IS NOT NULL` (`provisioning-jobs.ts:1501-1506`), and images without `POST /api/snapshot` return the `SNAPSHOT_ENDPOINT_UNSUPPORTED` sentinel, treated as a **benign skip** (`eliza-sandbox.ts:4125-4133`). Given `eliza-sandbox.ts:317-324`'s present-tense claim that the deployed V2 agent image lacks the route, **this population may be the majority of the running fleet right now** — for them the honest loss window is not "up to 6 h", it is *everything, always*. Phase 0 measures the population; Phase 1 makes the fleet-image rollout an explicit deliverable (§3).
2. **Persistently failing snapshots.** A large state that can't finish inside the 120 s pull timeout, or a chronically unhealthy bridge, fails every sweep; `last_backup_at` goes stale and nothing pages anyone (epic item B5's verifier covers decryptability of *existing* backups, not staleness).
3. **Sweep starvation — reachable today, at any cadence.** The due-set query is `.where(...).limit(maxAgents)` with **no `ORDER BY`** (`provisioning-jobs.ts:1484-1504`), so which 200 due rows get picked each tick is planner-dependent and nondeterministic. Sentinel skips return `{success:false}` and never bump `last_backup_at` (`eliza-sandbox.ts:4125-4133` — correctly so, bumping would mask staleness), so every route-less agent stays **perpetually due** and permanently competes for the 200-row window. As the perpetually-due population approaches `maxAgents`, specific healthy agents can be starved of backups **indefinitely at the current 6 h cadence** — tightening the interval without fixing this multiplies the wasted budget. Fixing the sweep is an explicit Phase 1 deliverable (§3).

**Honest fleet-wide statement:** "up to 6 h" describes only the route-bearing, non-starved subset of the fleet. Until the Phase 1 image rollout completes and the sweep is fixed, the pre-rollout fleet's realistic loss window ranges from 6 h to *unbounded*, and no alert distinguishes the two.

---

## 2. Options analysis

### (a) Tighten the auto-backup interval for local-state agents (e.g. 15 min)

*Mechanism already exists*: the cron route accepts `?intervalMs=&max=`; a second fan-out on the existing `*/15 * * * *` cron slot (`wrangler.toml:58`) filtered to local-state agents (`environment_vars->>'ELIZA_AGENT_LOCAL_STATE' = '1'`) is a config-plus-small-query change.

- **RPO:** 6 h → ~15 min *for route-bearing agents*; a strict no-op for agents that 404 the endpoint — which is why this option is gated behind the image rollout (§3 Phase 1).
- **Consistency:** the *best* of all options — `dumpDataDir` under `runExclusive` is a coherent logical dump, and the existing manifest/restore path (hash-verified, refuses tampered bytes) is reused unchanged.
- **Cost at fleet scale:** the pull is always FULL state (no incremental fetch), base64-JSON over the bridge. For N local-state agents averaging D MB of state: `96 × N × D` MB/day through the provisioning worker + one KMS encrypt + a jsonb write each. At N=1,000, D=100 MB that is ~9.6 TB/day of pull traffic and ~150 snapshot-jobs/hour-equivalent load (est. 45 s/job, `maxAttempts 2`). `maxAgents=200`/tick caps a 15-min sweep at ~200 agents per tick — beyond that the fleet silently falls behind its own interval (and without the sweep ordering fix, *which* agents fall behind is nondeterministic).
- **Agent-side cost:** `runExclusive` blocks DB writes for the dump duration → a latency spike on the live chat path every 15 min; grows with DB size.
- **Retention caveat:** `MAX_BACKUPS=10` at 15-min cadence shrinks the retained history from ~2.5 days to **2.5 hours** unless `MAX_BACKUPS` is raised (which multiplies Postgres storage; incremental rows soften but don't remove this).
- **Blast radius:** no new infrastructure; risk concentrates in worker throughput and shared-Postgres storage/IO. Failure mode is visible (job failures), not silent.

### (b) Node-side incremental sync of the host volume to R2 (restic/rclone-style)

A per-node systemd timer/sidecar shipping `/data/agents/*` to R2 (S3-compatible; the Worker already has a `BLOB` R2 binding). Content-addressed dedup makes network cost ≈ churn *for the plain-file set* (see the spool caveat under §3 Phase 3 — dedup is **zero** for encrypted envelopes); 5–15 min cadence is cheap.

- **Consistency caveat — the honest one:** copying a **live PGlite data dir** file-by-file yields a torn `$PGDATA` (equivalent to copying a running Postgres without a backup barrier); the restore may be corrupt or refuse to start, and there is no `pg_start_backup` equivalent in PGlite. So a naive restic of the whole volume gives **crash-consistent-at-best, torn-at-worst** DB copies. The *rest* of the volume is fine: the media store is content-addressed (sha256 filenames, immutable), vault/config files are small atomic writes.
- **Workable shape:** exclude `.pgdata`, ship media + vault + config + workspace + the agent's **local backup envelopes** (`*.agent-backup.json` spool — already KMS-encrypted, hash-manifested, consistent because they embed a `dumpDataDir` dump). That turns (b) into a consistent design instead of a corrupt-restore lottery — provided the envelope writes become atomic first (§3 Phase 3).
- **Cost:** R2 ≈ $0.015/GB-mo, zero egress; node CPU for scans; per-agent (or per-node) restic repo keys must come from KMS with **escrow off-box** — a repo key that only lives on the node defeats the purpose. Same for the local-envelope KMS root key (`ELIZA_KMS_BACKEND=local` root-key resolution, `packages/security/src/kms/index.ts:87+`): shipping ciphertext whose only key died with the node is the #15310 incident again in new clothes.
- **Blast radius:** a new daemon on every node and a new *silent-rot* failure mode — it needs the same staleness alerting as (a), plus a periodically exercised restore drill. It also creates a **second backup format** unless restore is unified through the existing manifest path.

### (c) Hetzner Cloud volumes (+ snapshots) for agent containers

Why the app-container path exists but agents don't use it: `hetzner-volumes.ts` was built for **stateful project/app containers** — its only production consumer is coding containers (`coding-containers.ts:45,177`, `use_hetzner_volume: true`; migration `0077_containers_hetzner_volumes.sql`). The file and migration document the constraints that made it a non-starter for the agent fleet:

- **Placement:** Cloud volumes attach only to Cloud-provisioned nodes in the *same location* — "NOT across locations and NOT to auctioned/dedicated boxes" (`hetzner-volumes.ts:15-17`, migration 0077 header). The agent fleet's seed capacity is dedicated/auction Robot boxes (`CONTAINERS_DOCKER_NODES`; the epic's incident cluster 3 is literally about "agent robots"), with Cloud `ccx33` only for autoscaled burst (`containers-env.ts:586`). A durability mechanism that skips the permanent capacity is not a durability mechanism.
- **Density:** Hetzner caps **16 attached volumes per server**. Agent nodes run tens of containers per box; per-agent volumes cannot scale past 16 agents/node.
- **Snapshots don't exist:** the Hetzner Cloud API has **no volume-snapshot endpoint** (server images only — they capture local disks, not volumes; our `hetzner-cloud-api.ts` wraps none because there is none). So option (c) degrades to "network disk that outlives the server": good crash-consistency on node death (ext4 journal + PGlite power-loss recovery), but **no point-in-time history, no protection against volume-level corruption/deletion, no cross-location DR**, ~€0.44+/agent-mo minimum (10 GB floor), plus attach/detach orchestration.
- **Verdict:** fine for the low-count coding-container product it was built for; wrong shape for the agent fleet. Not recommended.

### (d) Steer dedicated agents to managed shared Postgres (`database_uri` mode)

Mechanism exists today: provision with `ELIZA_AGENT_LOCAL_STATE=0` → `computeManagedAgentDbEnv` injects `DATABASE_URL` = shared Railway Postgres. The DB is then **off-box by construction** (provider-side durability/PITR), leaving only media/vault/config/workspace on the volume — exactly the crash-safe file set that (b) syncs without any consistency caveat.

- **Why we left:** #8696 connection exhaustion (since mitigated by `POSTGRES_POOL_MAX=8/MIN=0`, `managed-eliza-config.ts:301-307`) and, decisively, **latency**: ~166 ms/query to Railway × dozens of serial queries per turn was the dominant dedicated-chat latency (`managed-eliza-config.ts:229-236`). Reversing the default re-imports that regression wholesale.
- **What it would take to be viable:** connection pooling at the edge (pgbouncer) + **regional co-location** of the DB with the Hetzner nodes (the latency is geography, not Postgres), or per-agent managed DBs (cost + provisioning surface). Consistency story is the best available (real Postgres, provider PITR).
- **Verdict:** not as a fleet-wide reversal; **yes as an opt-in "durable" tier** for agents whose owners value RPO≈0 for DB state over per-turn latency, and as the standing recommendation for agents that already tolerate shared-DB latency.

### (e) Continuous DB replication: WAL shipping, or row-level write-back (`WriteBackService`)

Two distinct sub-options; v1 conflated them and wrongly claimed no in-repo prior art.

**(e1) Litestream-equivalent WAL shipping — still not viable.** Litestream is SQLite-only. PGlite is an embedded single-connection WASM Postgres: it exposes no `archive_command`, no replication protocol, no `pg_receivewal`, and no external WAL-streaming API; `dumpDataDir` is its only supported consistent export. Building WAL shipping means forking PGlite's WASM VFS layer — out of proportion when the dump pipeline already provides consistent point-in-time exports. Revisit only if upstream PGlite ships a WAL-streaming API.

**(e2) Row-level write-back — prior art exists in-repo and deserves an honest look.** `plugins/plugin-sql/src/write-back/index.ts` ships `WriteBackService` — Electric's Pattern 1 (Online Writes): local PGlite writes are forwarded row-by-row to the cloud API (`{base}/api/v1/eliza/agents/{agentId}/write`, keyed by `ELIZA_CLOUD_WRITE_BASE_URL` / `ELIZA_CLOUD_SERVICE_KEY`), and Electric's `syncShapesToTables` read path (`ELIZA_ELECTRIC_SYNC_URL`) syncs confirmed rows back to PGlite. This is exactly the continuous-replication family — the question is whether hardening it makes continuous DB off-boxing viable without litestream.

As shipped it is **not a durability mechanism**, by its own design:
- fire-and-forget with an **in-memory** queue — queued writes die with the process (`index.ts:9-12`, `:54`);
- **drops writes after `MAX_RETRIES = 5` with a warning log** (`:27`, `:199-221`) — silent divergence, precisely the log-and-continue-fabricates-health failure mode the repo's error doctrine bans on data paths;
- coverage is **per-call-site enqueue**, not adapter-wide interception — any table or write path not routed through it is silently unprotected;
- no transactional boundaries (multi-row atomicity) and no established restore path (reconstructing a coherent PGlite from central Postgres via the Electric read path is not proven for all runtime tables, nor for DDL/migrations).

**Could hardening it change the recommendation?** Honestly: RPO≈seconds for DB state, with **no `runExclusive` dump pause**, beats any cadence option (a) can reach — and it is incremental engineering on an existing seam, not a PGlite fork. The gap list is concrete: a durable on-disk queue (same tmp+rename crash rules as Phase 3's spool), ack'd at-least-once delivery with server-side `writeId` dedup (the `writeId` already exists), **adapter-level interception so coverage is total-or-fail-fast**, DDL/migration handling, and a B5-style verified restore path. That is five real subsystems, and until "coverage is total" is machine-checkable, row-level write-back has the worst durability failure mode available: *looks protected, isn't*.

- **Verdict (changed from v1):** no longer dismissed as "no prior art / not viable" — **rejected from the B7 critical path, kept as the long-term direction.** The dump pipeline is a complete, hash-verified capture→encrypt→store→verify→restore chain that needs cadence/sweep/rollout work; hardened write-back is a partial pipeline needing five new subsystems plus a new verification story, and it covers only DB state (files still need Phase 2 regardless). File it as future epic work — the natural successor to Phase 3 for DB state — and revisit once B5 verification and the Phase 3 spool have landed.

### (f) Node-side atomic filesystem snapshot (LVM-thin/btrfs/ZFS, or `fsfreeze`) + off-box sync

The middle path v1 skipped between "file-by-file copy of live `.pgdata` is torn" and "exclude `.pgdata` entirely": a **point-in-time atomic** snapshot of `/data/agents` at the block/FS layer, then ship the frozen snapshot contents to R2. Atomic snapshot ⇒ **power-loss-consistent**; the container-crash row in §1 already relies on PGlite recovering from power loss, so a `.pgdata` restored from an atomic snapshot starts exactly as if the node had lost power at snapshot time — crash recovery, not a torn copy.

- **Unique property:** zero agent cooperation. This is **the only option on the table that also protects the route-less sentinel population** (worst case 1) — every other consistent-DB option requires the agent image to participate (`/api/snapshot`, spool, or write-back).
- **Honest costs:**
  - Requires `/data` on a snapshot-capable layer. Robot boxes are heterogeneous — typically ext4 on raw disk/md-RAID with no LVM thin pool; converting a live node's storage **in place** is a per-node data-migration/re-provision-scale operation, not a config change.
  - The no-storage-change variant, `fsfreeze` + copy, is only atomic *while frozen*: freezing for the full copy duration stalls writes for **every container on the node** (tens of agents) for minutes; freezing briefly requires a snapshot layer to copy from — which is the storage retrofit again. Realistic (f) therefore means snapshot-capable storage.
  - Restores are **crash-recovery restores**, not clean dumps: the PGlite stale-lock crash-loop (#11222/#15228) is reachable on every restore, and there is no manifest/hash verification unless the shipped snapshot is wrapped in one — otherwise (f) silently becomes a second, weaker backup format.
  - CoW space for deltas, snapshot lifecycle/monitoring on every node, and the same R2 + key-escrow work as (b) — a snapshot sitting on the dying disk is worth nothing.
- **Verdict: adopt conditionally, not as core.** (i) Make snapshot-capable `/data` (btrfs or LVM-thin) the provisioning standard for **new** agent nodes — it is nearly free at provision time and buys a permanent whole-node recovery layer. (ii) If Phase 0 shows the sentinel population is large **and** the Phase 1 image rollout stalls, FS-snapshot+sync on capable nodes is the stopgap that bounds that population's loss window. It is not the primary fix because the image rollout uses an existing, tested, hash-verified pipeline and yields clean-dump restores; (f) yields crash-recovery restores and demands per-node storage surgery on the existing fleet.

---

## 3. Recommendation

**Hybrid of (a) + spool-based (b), keeping the existing hash-verified manifest as the single restore format; (d) as an opt-in tier; (f) as a new-node storage standard + conditional stopgap; reject (c); defer (e2) as the long-term successor for DB state.**

### Phase 0 — measure and alert (no behavior change)
- Fleet metrics: distribution of `last_backup_at` staleness for running local-state agents; count of running local-state agents with **zero** backups, split by cause (`bridge_url IS NULL` vs `SNAPSHOT_ENDPOINT_UNSUPPORTED` sentinel — the latter is the route-less-image population that gates Phase 1); snapshot size p50/p95/max vs the 120 s pull timeout; snapshot job failure rate; per-tick due-set size vs `maxAgents` (starvation pressure).
- **Alert (owner escalation, not a log line)** when any running local-state agent's newest backup age exceeds 2× its target interval, and on any never-backed-up running agent. Fail-fast doctrine: a stale or absent backup is an *error state*, not a warning — extends epic item B5's restorability verifier with staleness.

### Phase 1 — make the existing pipeline actually cover the fleet, then tighten it

Ordered deliverables — the cron change is last because it is a no-op against a fleet the pipeline can't reach:

1. **Fix the sweep (starvation).** Add `ORDER BY last_backup_at ASC NULLS FIRST` to the due-set query (`provisioning-jobs.ts:1484-1504`) so the window always serves the stalest agents first, and stop re-enqueueing known-unsupported images every tick: track `last_backup_attempt_at` separately (bumped on *every* attempt, including sentinel skips, while `last_backup_at` continues to bump only on durable success so staleness alerting stays honest), or equivalently a `snapshot_unsupported` marker cleared on image upgrade. Exit criterion: no running route-bearing agent's `last_backup_at` staleness exceeds 2× its target interval across a full sweep cycle, regardless of the sentinel population size.
2. **Fleet image rollout (closes worst case 1).** Move all running local-state dedicated agents onto an image that serves `POST /api/snapshot`, via the existing upgrade path (pre-upgrade snapshots already gate on a full manifest where available). **Measurable exit criterion: zero `SNAPSHOT_ENDPOINT_UNSUPPORTED` skips across a full sweep cycle, and 100% of running local-state agents hold ≥1 restorable (decrypt + hash-verify, per B5) backup no older than their target interval.** Until this exits, the fleet's real RPO is *not* 6 h and must not be reported as such; if Phase 0 finds the route-less population is the majority, this rollout — not the cron change — **is** the Phase 1 RPO win.
3. **Tighten the interval (RPO 6 h → 15–30 min for the covered fleet).** Fan `agent-backups` on the existing `*/15` cron slot (`wrangler.toml:58`) with `intervalMs` ≈ 15–30 min **scoped to local-state dedicated agents** (env-var filter in `enqueueScheduledBackups`); keep 6 h for shared-DB agents (their volume holds only files). Raise `MAX_BACKUPS` for the tightened cohort so the retention horizon isn't gutted (10 × 15 min = 2.5 h of history); lean on the existing incremental planner for storage. Gate on Phase 0 numbers: per-tick concurrency cap, worker headroom, and measured `runExclusive` dump-pause impact on live chat latency (abort the rollout if p95 turn latency regresses).

### Phase 2 — node-side R2 sync of the crash-safe file set (closes the node-death file gap)
- restic/rclone timer per node shipping `/data/agents/<id>` **excluding the live `.pgdata`** (media store is content-addressed and immutable — ideal for incremental sync; vault/config/workspace are small atomic files) to R2 every 5–15 min.
- Key management is a first-class deliverable: restic repo keys and the agent-local KMS root key must be escrowed off-box (Steward/KMS), never volume-resident-only — otherwise this rebuilds the #15310 undecryptable-backup incident.
- **R2 is backup/restore only, never a serve path.** The content-addressed media store remains the single file store (root `CLAUDE.md` / #8876); nothing may serve bytes from the R2 copy or grow a second storage abstraction around it.
- DB durability continues to come from Phase 1 dumps (consistent by construction); Phase 2 never restores a `.pgdata` copied live.
- New-node storage standard from option (f): provision new agent nodes with snapshot-capable `/data` (btrfs or LVM-thin) so whole-node FS-snapshot recovery is available where it is cheap, and as the stopgap lever if the Phase 1 rollout stalls.

#### Restore composition & skew (binding for the restorer)
Between Phase 1 and Phase 3, DB durability (control-plane dump taken at T1) and file durability (R2 sync taken at T2) come from different clocks; a node-death restore stitched from both is cross-component skewed. Rules:
- **Precedence:** a complete, hash-verified envelope (control-plane backup with full manifest, or a Phase 3 spool envelope) always wins over any stitched restore; among complete envelopes, newest verified wins. A stitched Phase1+Phase2 restore is a fallback only when no complete envelope exists or the newest one predates both parts.
- **Which wins on skew:** in a stitched restore, the DB dump (T1) is authoritative for structured state; the R2 file set (T2) is authoritative for file bytes. Neither is "merged".
- **How the restorer detects skew:** compare T1 vs T2, then verify that every media sha256 referenced from the restored DB resolves in the restored media store — content addressing makes this check exact. DB-referenced-but-missing objects are enumerated; unreferenced extra objects are harmless (the existing GC path owns them).
- **A skewed restore is a *degraded* restore:** surface "DB from T1, files from T2, K missing media objects" to the owner and mark the sandbox restore-degraded — never silently drop, fabricate, or quietly proceed. This extends the no-silent-rewind rule below.

### Phase 3 — write-through spool (structural fix; removes the live-pull single point)
- The agent already writes KMS-encrypted, hash-manifested local backup envelopes (`createLocalAgentBackup`). Schedule that *in the agent* (e.g. every 15 min into a bounded spool dir) and let the Phase 2 node sync ship the spool. The control-plane `/api/snapshot` pull then becomes the *verification* path rather than the only capture path — an agent that is briefly unreachable at sweep time no longer misses its RPO.
- **Atomic spool writes are a deliverable, not an assumption.** `createLocalAgentBackup` today writes the envelope with a plain `fs.writeFile` (`agent-backup.ts:875`). Phase 3 must switch it to tmp+rename: write `<name>.agent-backup.json.tmp` in the same directory, fsync, `rename(2)`, fsync the directory — and the node-side sync must ship only complete files (exclude `*.tmp`). Without this, a sweep can ship a torn *newest* envelope; hash verification makes it fail loudly at restore, but the effective RPO silently widens to the previous envelope.
- **The spool's transfer cost belongs to this recommendation** (not just to option (a)): envelopes are KMS-AES-GCM ciphertext of full state, so the bytes change completely every run and restic/rclone dedup is **zero** for the spool. Naive Phase 3 at 15-min cadence therefore re-imports option (a)'s `96 × N × D` MB/day math as R2 upload *and* doubles it as node-volume writes. Mitigations, in order:
  1. **Incremental envelopes (mandatory deliverable):** reuse the existing full-or-incremental planner shape at the component level — per-component manifests let unchanged components (media, workspace, vault, config — content-addressed or rarely-churning) be *referenced*, not re-shipped; only the DB dump component is inherently full each run.
  2. **Cadence scaling by state size** for large-state agents, with the staleness alerting keeping them honest.
  3. Chunked/**convergent encryption is explicitly rejected**: it leaks ciphertext equality across snapshots and tenants — a confidentiality trade we don't need once (1) exists.
- Restore stays unified: one manifest format, restore **refuses** partial/tampered components (component sha256 verification already does this — keep it), and any restore that isn't byte-complete **fails loudly**. On node-death recovery, surface "restored from backup taken at T; potential loss window X" to the owner — never a silent rewind (this also covers the re-provision-while-disk-was-fine rewind case in the table above).

### Cost of the recommended path (charged where it belongs)

| Component | Steady-state transfer | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 tightened pulls | `96 × N × D`/day worst-case through the worker | bounded by cohort scoping + `maxAgents`; full-state pulls, no dedup; visible-failure mode |
| Phase 2 file sync (media/vault/config/workspace) | ≈ churn only | content-addressed dedup works here |
| Phase 3 spool, naive | `96 × N × D`/day to R2 **+ the same again as node-volume writes** | encrypted full-state envelopes defeat dedup entirely — **unacceptable; why incremental envelopes are mandatory** |
| Phase 3 spool, with incremental envelopes | ≈ `96 × N × D_db`/day + file churn (D_db = compressed DB dump size) | the honest run-rate of the recommendation |

### What to measure throughout
- **Actual RPO**: age of the newest *restorable* (decrypt + hash-verify) backup, sampled fleet-wide — not `last_backup_at` alone.
- Sentinel-population count (must reach 0 to exit Phase 1.2) and per-tick due-set size vs `maxAgents` (starvation pressure, must stay < 1 after Phase 1.1).
- Snapshot pull duration p95 vs timeout; dump-pause impact on message-turn latency; worker queue depth per tick.
- Storage growth: `agent_sandbox_backups` (Postgres) and R2 (split file-set vs spool), per cohort.
- Restore-drill success rate: extend the `hetzner-sleep-wake-smoke` provision→destroy→restore drill (epic item A2) to also exercise a Phase 2/3 spool restore **and a stitched skewed restore** nightly.

### Did the recommendation shift after revision?

**The core did not; the path to it did.** The shape — tightened dump cadence + spool-shipped node sync unified on the hash-verified manifest, (d) opt-in, (c) rejected — survives because every alternative still fails on its own terms: (b)-naive and (f) produce crash-recovery-at-best DB copies where the dump path produces clean verified dumps; (c) cannot reach the permanent Robot capacity; (e2), even hardened, needs five new subsystems and total-coverage proof where the dump pipeline needs cadence/sweep/rollout work on a chain that already exists end-to-end. What shifted: **Phase 1 is no longer "a cron change"** — the sweep fix and the fleet-image rollout now precede and gate the interval tightening, because against the pre-rollout fleet the cron change alone protects nobody who isn't already protected; **(f) enters** as a new-node storage standard and conditional stopgap for the sentinel population; **(e2)'s rejection is narrowed** from "not viable / no prior art" to "not the B7 critical path", with `WriteBackService` named as the long-term DB-state successor; and **Phase 3 now owns its true transfer cost**, with atomic spool writes and incremental envelopes as explicit deliverables rather than assumptions.

## 4. Explicitly out of scope
- **Idle-freeze / auto-sleep cost optimization** — deferred by owner directive (see epic #15603 header).
- Wake-on-request routing, backup-restorability verification internals (B5), and restore-integrity-gate-on-wake (B6) — tracked separately in the epic.
- Hardening `WriteBackService` into a durability mechanism (e2) — future epic work, not B7.
